A.explanation: This is $1000$ times too small because $250\text{ mm}^2$ was not correctly converted to $2.5 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2$.

B.explanation: Using force per rod of $2500\text{ N}$, stress $1.0 \times 10^7\text{ Pa}$ and strain $5.0 \times 10^{-5}$ gives $E = 2.0 \times 10^{11}\text{ N m}^{-2}$.

C.explanation: This uses the full $10\text{ kN}$ instead of the share per rod and also mis-converts $\text{mm}^2$ to $\text{m}^2$.

D.explanation: This uses the full $10\text{ kN}$ on one rod area, giving four times the correct stress and Young modulus.

hints: Notice the $10\text{ kN}$ weight is equally supported by four rods, so first find the compressive force $F$ in one $2.0\text{ m}$ rod.
Recall $E = \text{stress}/\text{strain} = (F/A)/(x/L)$ and that $A = 250\text{ mm}^2$ and $x = 0.10\text{ mm}$ must both be converted to metres.
Compare stress from $F$ in newtons over $A$ in $\text{m}^2$ with strain from $0.10 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}$ over $2.0\text{ m}$ before dividing.
walkthrough: The load is shared, so force on one rod is $F = 10000/4 = 2500\text{ N}$ in compression. Hooke's law still applies with magnitudes.

Convert to SI units: $A = 250\text{ mm}^2 = 250 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2 = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2$ and extension magnitude $x = 0.10\text{ mm} = 0.10 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m} = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}$.
Stress in one rod is $\text{stress} = F/A = 2500/(2.5 \times 10^{-4}) = 1.0 \times 10^7\text{ N m}^{-2}$.
Strain in one rod is $\text{strain} = x/L = (1.0 \times 10^{-4})/2.0 = 5.0 \times 10^{-5}$, with no unit.
Young modulus is $E = \text{stress}/\text{strain} = (1.0 \times 10^7)/(5.0 \times 10^{-5}) = 2.0 \times 10^{11}\text{ N m}^{-2}$. This is option B.
